passage:
Chen had lost four chess games in a row on the puzzle site, the last one in only nine moves. He slumped at the kitchen table of their Singapore flat, cheeks hot.
A chat bubble appeared from his opponent, Olga: "hey, are you ok? that was a rough game. I lose like that all the time 🙂"
Chen blinked. A stranger had noticed. He typed, "thanks, I'm ok. you played really well."
"want a tip? castle early!"
They played one friendly game, and Chen lasted twenty moves. Then Olga wrote, "what city are u in? I'm in Riga."
Chen smiled but typed, "I keep that private, sorry. thanks for being nice though!"
"no problem, good luck!"
At dinner he told his dad about the kind player.

qa.q: How many moves did Chen's last lost game take?
qa.a: Only nine moves.

qa.q: How did Chen feel when Olga asked if he was okay?
qa.a: He felt surprised and comforted; after losing so badly, it was nice that a stranger noticed.

qa.q: How did Chen balance friendliness and safety?
qa.a: He chatted kindly and took the tip, but kept his city private and told his dad about the player.

qa.q: How might Olga see Chen's choice to keep his city private?
qa.a: Olga accepted it easily with "no problem, good luck", which is how a kind player responds; pushing for details would have been a warning sign.

grounding: A boy comforted by a kind stranger after a bad loss stays friendly but does not share private information.

passage:
At the community centre's Saturday game hour, Urmila crashed out of the word-battle round in last place. The screen flashed LOSER in big red letters. She pressed her lips together so nobody would see them wobble.
A message popped up from another player, Kite22: "that round was super hard, u ok? ur spelling of rhythm was great tho"
Urmila smiled for the first time that morning. "thx. im ok now."
She liked this player. She began typing, "want my number so we can..." and stopped.
Parveen didi, the volunteer at the next desk, glanced over. "Nice message, na?"
"Very nice. Should I give my number?"
"Chat in the game if you like. Numbers and names stay private, even with nice people."
Urmila deleted the line and typed, "gg, see u next week".

qa.q: What did the screen flash after Urmila crashed out?
qa.a: LOSER in big red letters.

qa.q: What does Urmila's wobbling lip suggest she felt before the message came?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and sad about coming last.

qa.q: Which choice kept Urmila safe while she enjoyed the kindness?
qa.a: She deleted the offer of her number and kept the chat inside the game.

qa.q: How might Parveen didi see Urmila's question about the number?
qa.a: Parveen didi sees a child touched by kindness and gently reminds her that private details stay private, even with nice people.

grounding: A girl cheered by a stranger's kind message after losing stays friendly but keeps her number and name private.

passage:
In Sironj, the afternoon power cut had made the house hot and slow. Nirmala was looking at her drawings on Amma's old phone when a message arrived: "Hi! I saw your peacock drawing. Where did you learn? I'm Bhavna 🙂"
Nirmala sat up. Someone liked her peacock! She wanted to ask who Bhavna was, where she lived, whether she drew too. Her thumb hovered over the keys.
Then she carried the phone to the courtyard, where Amma was sorting red chillies. "Amma, someone I don't know messaged me. Can I reply?"
Amma read it slowly. "We don't know who this is. You can say thank you, but no school name, no address, no photos. And show me whatever comes next."
Nirmala typed "thank you" and handed the phone back.

qa.q: Which drawing did the message mention?
qa.a: Nirmala's peacock drawing.

qa.q: What did Nirmala want when the message arrived?
qa.a: She felt curious and excited, wanting to know who Bhavna was, where she lived and whether she drew too.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do before replying, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She showed Amma first, so an adult could decide what was safe to say.

qa.q: How does Amma see the message?
qa.a: Amma sees someone unknown, so she allows only a thank-you and asks to see anything that comes next.

grounding: A girl is curious about a stranger's friendly message but checks with her mother before replying and shares no private details.

passage:
In Valencia, Clara was practising violin with a music app when a new message blinked: "Hi Clara! Nice video of your scales. How long have you been playing? I play cello."
Clara's heart jumped. A cello player! She had a hundred questions. Her little brother Pablo, lying on the rug with his cars, said, "Just answer, it's only music."
"Maybe," Clara said. She wanted to. But she didn't know this person, and the message had used her name.
She took the tablet to Mamá in the kitchen. Mamá read it and frowned slightly. "Your name is showing on your videos. Let's hide it first. Then we decide together whether you answer. And never your school, our address or photos."
Together they changed the settings. Clara still felt curious, but calmer.

qa.q: What instrument did the message writer say they played?
qa.a: The cello.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when the message blinked?
qa.a: She felt excited and curious, with a hundred questions to ask.

qa.q: What steps did Clara and Mamá take before any reply?
qa.a: They hid Clara's name on the videos and agreed to decide together, with no school, address or photos shared.

qa.q: Why might Pablo react differently from Clara?
qa.a: Pablo sees it as "only music", while Clara noticed that a stranger knew her name, which made her pause.

grounding: A girl curious about a stranger's message checks with her mother before chatting and keeps her school, address and photos private.

passage:
I'm Binita. A few weeks ago, someone in my drawing game started sending me messages. At first they were just nice: "Your art is amazing." Then: "You're so mature, not like other kids. You're special." I felt flattered. Nobody had ever called me mature before.
Then, one morning before school, a message said, "Let's keep our chats secret. Grown-ups won't understand us."
My stomach went cold. A secret from Mummy? I didn't reply. At the first break I told Maria Miss, my voice shaking. She listened to everything, then said, "You have done nothing wrong. Telling me was brave." She called Mummy that same afternoon, and at home we saved the messages, blocked the account and reported it together.
I still draw. I just don't chat with strangers any more.

qa.q: What did the message say grown-ups would not do?
qa.a: It said grown-ups won't understand them.

qa.q: How did Binita's feelings change when the stranger asked for secrecy?
qa.a: Binita went from flattered to frightened; the cold stomach showed that something felt wrong.

qa.q: What did Maria Miss do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, told Binita that nothing was Binita's fault, and called Mummy the same afternoon so the messages were saved, blocked and reported.

qa.q: Why might the stranger have praised Binita so much before asking for secrecy?
qa.a: The praise was meant to make Binita feel special and trusting, so a secret would feel like part of the friendship.

grounding: A child flattered by an online stranger who then asks for secrecy recognises the red flag, stops replying and tells a teacher, who acts that day.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Wednesday
Santosh came to my room at lunch with his friend Jahnavi, who kept a hand on his sleeve and said, "Just tell. It's okay."
Santosh showed me messages on his mother's old phone from someone in a homework-help group: "You're smarter than kids your age." "You're special to me." "Don't tell your parents about our chats, they'll spoil it."
He said he had stopped replying but felt he had done something bad. I told him clearly that he had done nothing wrong and that coming to me was exactly right. We took screenshots together. I phoned his mother before school ended; she came in, and we blocked and reported the account and informed the school's safeguarding lead that afternoon.
When he left, Santosh's shoulders had dropped. Jahnavi walked him back to class.

qa.q: Where did the messages come from?
qa.a: Someone in a homework-help group.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and worried, believing he had done something bad.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do the same day?
qa.a: They told him it was not his fault, took screenshots with him, phoned his mother, blocked and reported the account and informed the safeguarding lead.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi see her friend's situation?
qa.a: Jahnavi could see Santosh needed help, so she encouraged him to speak and stayed close to him.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a boy flattered and asked for secrecy by an online stranger, who stops replying and is told he did nothing wrong.

passage:
Monday: A player in Vikas's racing game kept asking questions. "Which school? Which area?" Vikas ignored them and kept racing.
Wednesday: A new message appeared: "I know where you live. Nice blue gate." Vikas froze. His hands went cold. Their gate was blue. He did not type a single word. He took a screenshot, the way his cousin Pooja had once shown him, and ran to the kitchen. "Mummy, look."
Mummy read it, put down the ladle and held him tight. "You did everything right. This is not your fault." That evening she and Papa reported and blocked the account and called the cyber-crime helpline, who took down the screenshots.
Saturday: Vikas still glanced at the gate sometimes. But Papa had locked down his settings, and Vikas's chest felt looser when he played.

qa.q: What colour gate did the message mention?
qa.a: A blue gate.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he read the message?
qa.a: He was terrified; he froze and his hands went cold.

qa.q: Which steps did Vikas take, and why were they right?
qa.a: He did not reply, took a screenshot and told Mummy at once, so adults could report it and get help that evening.

qa.q: How did Mummy see the moment Vikas showed her the message?
qa.a: Mummy was worried but calm; she held him, told him it was not his fault and acted the same evening.

grounding: A boy frightened by a stranger claiming to know where he lives saves the message, does not answer and tells a trusted adult immediately.

passage: Tanuja, you look pale. Did something online scare you? Then listen to your Yogesh Mama first. When I was about your age, we had one computer in the corner of the hall, and I chatted on a cricket forum. One night a stranger wrote, "I know your house. Near the temple tank, isn't it?" I went stiff. I couldn't even move the mouse. And being scared was the right feeling, Tanuja; it tells you something is wrong. I didn't answer. I shouted for my father. He printed every message, sat beside me till I slept, and the next morning we went to the police station together. They took it seriously. Nothing ever happened, but I learnt to tell someone at once. So, show me what you got, and we will call your Amma right now.

qa.q: Where did the stranger claim young Yogesh lived?
qa.a: Near the temple tank.

qa.q: How did young Yogesh feel when he read the message?
qa.a: Terrified; he went stiff and could not even move the mouse.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Mama's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Not replying and shouting for his father straight away; that let an adult save the messages and take them to the police.

qa.q: How might young Yogesh's father have felt that night?
qa.a: He was probably alarmed but steady, printing every message and sitting with his son before going to the police.

grounding: An uncle recalls freezing when a stranger claimed to know his house, and how not replying and telling an adult at once brought help.

passage:
Diary, Friday night
I've been hiding something all week. A person in my game chat called Tigerclaw asked where I study, and I TOLD them. We chatted every night after that. Mumma had said no chatting with strangers. My tummy has hurt for days.
Tonight Bidisha didi found me crying in the bathroom. She said, "Whatever it is, Mumma will help. Come."
I told Mumma with my eyes on the floor. I waited for shouting. Instead she held my face and said, "Thank you for telling me. We are on your side, always." We blocked Tigerclaw together, and Papa wrote to the school so they know.
I feel so much lighter. I wish I had said it on the first day.
Yash

qa.q: What did Yash tell Tigerclaw?
qa.a: Where Yash studies.

qa.q: Why did Yash hide the chats all week?
qa.a: Yash felt ashamed and scared of being shouted at for breaking Mumma's rule.

qa.q: What made telling Mumma easier, and what could Yash do sooner next time?
qa.a: Bidisha didi's push helped; next time Yash could tell on the first day, since Mumma was on Yash's side.

qa.q: How did Mumma see Yash's confession?
qa.a: Mumma was grateful to be told and saw it as a reason to protect Yash, not to punish.

grounding: A child ashamed of chatting with a stranger is afraid to tell a parent, then finds that telling brings relief and support.

passage:
In Kalamb, Pranav had been quiet for three days. Even the buffalo calf's antics didn't make him laugh. On Baba's phone he had chatted with a stranger from a video-site comment section and sent the name of their village, though Baba had warned him never to.
His cousin Nilesh cornered him by the well. "You look like you swallowed a stone. What happened?"
Pranav whispered it all. "Baba will be so angry."
"He'll be more upset if he finds out later. Come, I'll stand with you."
They found Baba in the cowshed. Pranav's voice shook as he spoke. Baba listened, wiped his hands and pulled him close. "Arre, beta, you were carrying this alone? We'll block this person right now. Next time, come straight to me. I am always on your side."

qa.q: What did Pranav send the stranger?
qa.a: The name of their village.

qa.q: What does Pranav's quietness over three days suggest?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid, carrying a secret and dreading Baba's anger.

qa.q: What helped Pranav speak up, and what did Baba do?
qa.a: Nilesh offered to stand with him; Baba listened, comforted him and blocked the person straight away.

qa.q: How did Baba feel when he heard Pranav's secret?
qa.a: Baba seemed sad that Pranav had carried it alone, not angry, and wanted him to come straight to him next time.

grounding: A boy ashamed of chatting with a stranger fears telling his father, then finds his father is on his side.

passage: Jasleen, you want to know if telling on a friend is ever right? Your Rukmini Bua learnt that at your age. My best friend Mitu had a secret: someone from a chat room who called her beautiful and kept asking for photos. She told me at lunch and begged, "Don't tell anyone. You're my best friend." All afternoon my stomach churned. After the last bell I went back inside and told our class teacher everything. The teacher thanked me, found Mitu at the gate, and phoned Mitu's mother that same evening. Mitu didn't speak to me for a week. She was furious. Then one evening she came to our gate and said, "Thank you. That person was scary." We are still friends, Jasleen.

qa.q: What did the stranger keep asking Mitu for?
qa.a: Photos.

qa.q: Why did young Rukmini's stomach churn all afternoon?
qa.a: She felt torn and anxious, caught between Mitu's plea for secrecy and fear for Mitu's safety.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bua's story?
qa.a: Going back after the last bell to tell the class teacher, who acted that same evening so Mitu was protected.

qa.q: How did Mitu see Rukmini's choice, first and later?
qa.a: At first Mitu was furious, but later she was grateful and admitted that the person was scary.

grounding: An aunt recalls that loyalty to a friend chatting secretly with a stranger meant telling a trusted adult, even though the friend was angry.

passage:
The school bus was already rumbling when Leena grabbed Harsha's arm. "Promise you won't tell. My online friend wants a photo of me tonight, just for him. He says I'm his best friend."
"Leena, that's not a friend."
"Promise!" she snapped, and climbed aboard.
Harsha stood frozen as the bus pulled away. Tonight. The holidays started tomorrow, and there would be no teachers for ten days. Leena would be furious with him. But she might get hurt.
He ran back through the gate to the staff room, where Thomas Sir was packing up. Out of breath, Harsha told him everything. Thomas Sir listened, thanked him, and phoned Leena's mother right there, before the bus had even reached her stop.
"You were a real friend today," he said.

qa.q: When did the online friend want Leena's photo?
qa.a: Tonight.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling as the bus pulled away?
qa.a: He felt torn and scared: Leena would be furious, but she might get hurt.

qa.q: Why did it matter that Harsha acted at once?
qa.a: The holidays started the next day, so telling Thomas Sir right away meant Leena's mother was phoned before that night.

qa.q: How might Leena see Harsha's choice at first?
qa.a: She will probably feel angry and betrayed, since she made him promise, even though he did it to keep her safe.

grounding: A boy learns his friend is secretly being asked for photos by a stranger and chooses her safety over the secret by telling a teacher at once.

passage:
Tuesday night
At six today Tanuja posted in our class group: "Ojas smells like a dustbin, nobody sit near Ojas tomorrow." Eleven people reacted. ELEVEN. It felt like everyone was staring at me through the phone.
I typed a long mean answer about her teeth. Then I deleted it. Papa always says never fight in the group.
I took screenshots instead, even though my hands were shaking, and showed Papa. He read it twice, then sat next to me on the bed. "This is not your fault, and you were right not to reply." He wrote to our class teacher tonight with the screenshots, and she has already answered that she will speak to the class tomorrow.
I still feel sick about going to school. But not alone.
Ojas

qa.q: How many people reacted to Tanuja's post?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after seeing the post?
qa.a: Ojas felt hurt and exposed, as if everyone was staring through the phone.

qa.q: Which choices helped Ojas, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the angry reply, saving screenshots and showing Papa, who wrote to the class teacher that night.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see her post compared with Ojas?
qa.a: Tanuja may think it is just a joke for laughs, while for Ojas it is public and deeply hurtful.

grounding: A child mocked in a class group chat feels hurt and exposed, saves proof instead of replying and tells a parent, who contacts the teacher.

passage:
The class group on Ma's phone buzzed during dinner in their small house near the Rewa bus stand. Hrithik had posted a voice note: someone copying Ankita reading English aloud, stretching every word, with the caption "Our Ankita, newsreader!" Laughing replies piled up underneath.
Ankita's face burned. She wanted to vanish under the charpai. She also wanted to send something nasty back.
Instead, she held the phone out. "Ma, listen."
Ma listened once, pressed her lips together, and helped Ankita save the voice note and the replies. Then she called the class teacher, who promised to remove the post that night and speak to Hrithik's parents. "It's not your fault, bitiya," Ma said, stroking her hair.

qa.q: What caption did Hrithik post with the voice note?
qa.a: "Our Ankita, newsreader!"

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when the voice note played?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and exposed; her face burned and she wanted to vanish.

qa.q: What did Ankita and her mother do instead of replying?
qa.a: They saved the voice note and the replies and called the class teacher that night.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the post compared with Ankita?
qa.a: Hrithik may think it was a harmless joke, but for Ankita it was public and painful.

grounding: A girl mocked by a classmate in a group chat feels exposed, saves the proof instead of replying, and tells her mother, who contacts the teacher.

passage:
I'm Ramesh, and during the summer holidays I asked the AI helper on Papa's laptop about a hundred questions. Why is the sea salty? How do bats find their way? Do octopuses have hearts? Every answer came in a blink, like a genie. I loved it.
Then my friend Asif and I made a poster about octopuses for school. The AI had said an octopus has two hearts. Asif's library book said three. We stared at each other. "Who's right?" Asif asked. We showed Sultana Miss, who opened a second book. Three hearts!
Now I still ask the AI loads of things, but for school work I check with a book or a teacher too. It is still fun. It just isn't always right.

qa.q: How many hearts did Asif's library book say an octopus has?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel about the AI's instant answers at first?
qa.a: Ramesh was delighted and amazed, as if the AI were a genie.

qa.q: What habit did Ramesh build after the octopus mix-up?
qa.a: To keep asking the AI but check school facts with a book or a teacher.

qa.q: How might Asif have seen the moment the two answers clashed?
qa.a: Asif was puzzled and curious about who was right, which led them to ask Sultana Miss.

grounding: A child loves an AI assistant's instant answers and learns to double-check with books and teachers because it can be wrong.

passage:
Library period note, Friday
Kashish spent the whole period at the library computer asking the AI tool about volcanoes, one question after another, bouncing on the chair. "It answers before I finish thinking!" she told Uma. When it said the big hill outside our town was an active volcano, Uma frowned. Her uncle had climbed it many times; it was just rock.
Kashish looked unsure, so I suggested they check. Together we opened the geography atlas and a children's encyclopedia: the hill is not a volcano at all.
Kashish laughed. "So it can be wrong!" She wrote a new rule on her notebook cover: "Ask AI, then check." I have asked her to share it with the class on Monday.

qa.q: What rule did Kashish write on her notebook cover?
qa.a: "Ask AI, then check."

qa.q: How did Kashish feel while asking the AI questions?
qa.a: She felt excited and delighted, bouncing on the chair because it answered so fast.

qa.q: What did the library teacher suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: They suggested checking the atlas and encyclopedia, which showed the AI's mistake without spoiling Kashish's curiosity.

qa.q: How did Uma see the AI's answer?
qa.a: Uma doubted it, because her uncle had climbed the hill many times and knew it was just rock.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a curious girl enjoying an AI's quick answers and learning to double-check with books because it can be wrong.

passage:
In Niphad, Mohit had twelve fraction sums for homework and a cricket match waiting. He borrowed his cousin Nikita's phone, typed the sums into the AI helper, and copied the answers in ten minutes. What a relief! He ran to the ground.
Next morning Kale Sir called him to the board. "Mohit, show us number four."
Mohit held the chalk. The numbers swam. He had written the answer, but he didn't know how he got it. The class waited. His ears went hot.
That evening he asked Nikita for the phone again, but this time he typed, "Explain how to add fractions with different bottom numbers. Don't give answers." He worked through two sums himself, slowly, on the back of an old calendar. The third one came out right.

qa.q: How many fraction sums did Mohit have for homework?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling at the board?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and panicky; the numbers swam and his ears went hot.

qa.q: How did Mohit change the way he used the AI?
qa.a: He asked it to explain the method without giving answers, then did the sums himself.

qa.q: How might Kale Sir see Mohit at the board?
qa.a: Kale Sir could see that Mohit had answers but no understanding, a sign the homework was not really his own work.

grounding: A boy relieved to let an AI do his homework cannot explain it in class, then uses it to explain the method and tries the work himself.

passage:
In Hanoi, Tuan had a book report due Monday and a new puzzle game calling. On Sunday he asked the AI to write the report. It produced a neat page in seconds. Tuan printed it and felt light as a kite.
At Monday's reading circle, Ms. Linh asked, "Tuan, why do you think the girl in the story ran away?" Tuan opened his mouth. Nothing came. He hadn't finished the book. Beside him, his friend Emil answered easily.
After school Tuan sat at his desk. He asked the AI only one thing: "What are good questions to think about when reading a story?" Then he read the last three chapters himself and wrote a new report, short and messy but all his own. He handed it to Ms. Linh the next day.

qa.q: What did Ms. Linh ask Tuan at the reading circle?
qa.a: Why he thought the girl in the story ran away.

qa.q: How did Tuan feel after printing the AI's report?
qa.a: He felt relieved and light, like a kite.

qa.q: What did Tuan do differently after the reading circle?
qa.a: He asked the AI for good questions to think about, read the chapters himself and wrote his own report.

qa.q: How might Ms. Linh see Tuan's second report?
qa.a: She may value it more than the neat one, because it shows his own reading and thinking.

grounding: A boy who lets an AI write his report cannot answer in class, then uses it only for guidance and does the work himself.

passage:
Thursday
Class quiz today. Question: "Can you see the Great Wall of China from the Moon with just your eyes?" I wrote YES in big letters, because last night the AI told me so, and it sounded SO sure. It even gave reasons.
Wrong. Our teacher explained that astronauts have said it is far too narrow to spot. Two people laughed. My ears went red.
At home Sonali apa said, "The AI isn't lying. It just sounds confident even when it's wrong." She showed me how to check with the encyclopedia and the science site our teacher recommends.
New rule for me: if it matters, check it twice. Still annoyed about that one mark. 😅
Asif

qa.q: What did Asif write for the Great Wall question?
qa.a: YES in big letters.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when the answer turned out wrong?
qa.a: Asif felt embarrassed, with red ears, and annoyed about losing the mark.

qa.q: What rule did Asif make, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: If it matters, check it twice, because an answer can sound confident and still be wrong.

qa.q: How does Sonali apa see the AI?
qa.a: Sonali apa sees it as a tool that sounds sure even when mistaken, not as a liar.

grounding: A child who believed an AI's confident answer learns that fluent answers can be wrong and starts checking important facts.

passage:
Pooja was writing a page on the old hill fort above their village for the district essay contest. On her brother Dhruv's phone she asked the AI who built it. The answer came instantly, full of names and dates, so confident that she copied it word for word.
On Sunday the family climbed up for a picnic. Dhruv stopped at the rusty signboard near the gate. "Pooja, look. This says a different king, and a hundred years later."
Pooja's face fell. "But it sounded so sure!"
The old caretaker, sweeping the steps, chuckled. "Sounding sure and being right are cousins, not twins."
That evening Pooja crossed out her paragraph. She checked the school library's district book, asked her history teacher, and rewrote it.

qa.q: Where did Dhruv find a different answer?
qa.a: On the rusty signboard near the gate.

qa.q: Why did Pooja's face fall at the signboard?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and a bit foolish, because she had trusted the AI just for sounding so sure.

qa.q: How did Pooja fix her essay?
qa.a: She checked the school library's district book, asked her history teacher and rewrote the paragraph.

qa.q: How does the caretaker see Pooja's mistake?
qa.a: The caretaker finds it gently funny and reminds her that sounding sure is not the same as being right.

grounding: A girl who trusted an AI because it sounded confident finds it was mistaken and learns to check important facts.
